paper_title: MLE-World: Predicting Machine Learning Experiment Outcomes with a Learned World Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: AI research agents repeatedly write programs, execute them, inspect terminal output, and revise solutions (Jiang et al., 2025; Nam et al., 2026), but this feedback is expensive because each step trains and evaluates model. Therefore, execution time limits how many ideas they can test (Toledo et al., 2026; Hambardzumyan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a), making cheap feedback and selective execution central to efficient search. Prior work prunes unpromising branches (Liu et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2026), predicts model performance (Kulibaba et al., 2025), or ranks candidates before execution (Zheng et al., 2026; Foster et al., 2026). Pruning and ranking can reduce total execution cost, but the cost per execution remains unchanged, and they do not provide terminal output, such as error traces and training logs, to guide subsequent debugging and program revision. The high cost of training makes machine learning engineering (MLE) natural setting for world models that predict execution feedback without running the program (Yang, 2026). MLE-World predicts candidate solutions terminal output from its code and the tasks data description. We finetune Qwen3.5-4B on logged pairs of code and output from successful and failed runs. One inference call predicts error traces, training logs, and the validation score, supporting both debugging and candidate selection. Cheap predicted feedback makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for MLE agents. TTS can scale along two dimensions: sampling more complete trajectories (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024) or taking more interaction steps within trajectory (Shen et al., 2025). In MLE, both require additional training runs, limiting search under fixed time budget. Prior agents execute every candidate (Nam et al., 2026) or rank candidates without execution feedback (Zheng et al., 2026). We focus on 2 MLE-World scaling interactions so the agent can adapt to feedback throughout the search. MLE-World makes this affordable by letting the agent compare several candidates using predicted error traces, training logs, and scores, then execute only the selected candidate. We build five policies on these predictions: Best-of-N (BoN), Sequential revision, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and rule based on upper confidence bounds (UCB). MLE-World also reports confidence score with each prediction, which serves search in two ways. First, it guides selection. Greedy selection by validation score can limit exploration (Toledo et al., 2026; Hambardzumyan et al., 2026) and overlook candidates the world model undervalues, so UCB adds an uncertainty bonus to predicted quality. Second, it decides when to trust prediction. Wrong predictions can mislead search (Janner et al., 2019), so confidence gate trusts confident predictions and runs the real execution. The gate works with any of the five policies. Across 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks (Chan et al., 2025), MLE-World matches observed terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs versus 41.1% for the best prompted baseline, with 131,061 less GPU inference time. MLE-World guided search achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without world model while reducing real execution. These results suggest that cheap feedback from world model enables test time scaling, improving agent performance by exploring more candidate programs. We summarize our main contributions as follows: An execution world model for MLE. We introduce MLE-World, 4B model that reads programs code and data description and predicts its terminal output, including crashes, training logs, and validation scores, outperforming much larger prompted models. World model guided test time scaling. We build five TTS policies that use MLE-World to select among several candidates per step by their predicted execution feedback, then run only the selected one. All five have higher observed mean percentiles than the agent without world model. Selective execution using model confidence. We run program for real only when MLEWorlds prediction has low confidence. Gating reduces real execution time while broadly maintaining performance.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: MLE agents. MLE agents reduce execution cost through pruning (Liu et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2026), performance prediction (Kulibaba et al., 2025), or candidate ranking (Foster et al., 2026; White et al., 2021). ForeAgent (Zheng et al., 2026) uses pairwise preference and confidence gate to select candidate for execution. Scores and preferences guide selection but lack error traces for debugging, which may require waiting for costly runs to fail. MLE-World predicts terminal output to support both selection and revision, using confidence to decide when real execution is needed. World models for LLM agents. World models predict an actions outcome without performing it (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Janner et al., 2019). LLM world models, prompted (Thimmaiah et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024) or trained on agent logs (Chae et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Zuo et al., 2026), serve web, computer use, and software agents. Closest to ours, DSWorld (Yang et al., 2026b) simulates individual steps in data science workflow and uses operation cost to decide when to simulate. MLE-World instead predicts complete programs terminal output, including error traces, training logs, and validation scores, to guide program search. It uses prediction confidence to decide when real execution is needed, targeting unreliable feedback rather than expensive operations alone. Test time scaling and search. Sampling (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024), tree search (Yao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023), revision (Shinn et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024), synthesis (Khairi et al., 2026), and longer interaction (Shen et al., 2025) require feedback to guide search. In MLE, slow training and evaluation limit this exploration. MLE-World predicts terminal output to guide candidate selection, revision, and synthesis, using confidence to determine when real execution is needed. 3 MLE-World

sections.title: 3.1 AGENT SCAFFOLD
sections.content: AIDE. We build on AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025) (although MLE-World is compatible with other agent scaffolds), the reference scaffold of MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025) and the base of most later MLE agents (Liu et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2026; Ou et al., 2025). AIDE searches for program that solves task τ over tree whose nodes are programs and whose edges are three operators: Draft writes new program, Debug rewrites buggy parent, and Improve makes one atomic change to valid parent. For fixed execution settings, the real executor returns terminal output = E(τ, s): training logs, the error trace on failure, and the validation score the program computes on held out split of the training data. An LLM parser reads and returns bug flag and the score. The policy drafts few initial solutions, debugs buggy nodes up to fixed depth, and otherwise improves the best valid node; the node with the best validation score is submitted and graded on the hidden test set against the leaderboard. Every node costs one execution.

sections.title: 3.2 WORLD MODELS FOR LLM AGENTS
sections.content: LLM world models. language world model predicts the observation resulting from an action without executing it (Chae et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2024). In the general formulation, an LLM world model conditions on the observationaction history (o1, a1, . . . , ot, at). Because each candidate program is self-contained, MLE-World uses only the current program and execution context to predict its terminal output, without requiring the preceding interaction history: ˆot+1 = fϕ(κ, ot, at). Here fϕ is the world model with parameters ϕ, and κ provides the context needed to predict the terminal output, such as the environment state. We treat the complete candidate program as the current observation ot and its execution as the action at. The model predicts the resulting terminal output as the next observation ˆot+1. Section 4 details the models input and structured output format.

sections.title: 5 SEARCH GUIDED BY MLE-WORLD
sections.content: We build five world model guided TTS policies on MLE-Worlds predictions (Section 5.1), then add confidence gate that works with any of them and decides when prediction needs real run (Section 5.2). 5.1 TEST TIME SCALING ON PREDICTED OUTPUTS Predicted outputs let step screen many candidates and run one. MLE-World stands in for execution when comparing candidates: step draws candidates, predicts their outputs ˆyi = hϕ(xi), and executes only one. Each of our five policies reads these predictions, not only the code (Figure 2; algorithms in Appendix J). Best-of-N (BoN) keeps the best predicted validation score (Brown et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2026). Sequential revises each candidate from the previous ones predicted error trace, log, and score, where prior revision uses real feedback (Snell et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2026). Pairwise extends ForeAgent (Zheng et al., 2026), which compares candidates without execution feedback: an LLM judge compares two candidates at time with their predicted terminal outputs until one remains. Fusion synthesizes new program from the pool and its predicted terminal outputs (Khairi et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026). UCB adds an exploration bonus from MLE-Worlds confidence to the predicted score, as described next. UCB: greedy selection can discard promising programs. BoN selects the best predicted validation score without accounting for prediction reliability. If MLE-World underestimates promising programs quality, greedy selection can discard it before execution provides feedback for subsequent search. Outcome uncertainty supplies an inexpensive exploration signal. GP-UCB balances estimated value with the objectives posterior standard deviation (Srinivas et al., 2009). We use outcome uncertainty u(x) as an empirical exploration proxy, not formal confidence bound. Lower confidence accompanies less accurate metric predictions on held out programs (Figure 7), so the bonus favors potentially underestimated candidates at no additional inference cost. sections.title: 5.2 EXECUTION GATING BY UNCERTAINTY
sections.content: Real runs are spent where predictions are least reliable. Predictions are cheap but not always right: on held out programs, 22% of predicted terminal outputs and 14% of predicted exception classes disagree with the real run  (Table 1)  , and such errors can mislead search (Janner et al., 2019). Because accuracy rises with confidence (Section 4), after any of the five policies selects candidate, the gate requests real feedback when pmax(xs (5) or when confidence is missing, where is the program returned by the search policy at step and γ (0, 1) is confidence threshold. Otherwise the predicted output guides the next Debug or Improve step. We always execute candidate with new best predicted validation metric, regardless of confidence, because the best verified candidate supplies the final submission. ) < γ, Thresholds follow the cost of each predicted outcome. We set γ = γs for predicted successes and γ = γf for failures, because their runs cost very different amounts of time. failing program usually crashes within seconds, so we can afford to run many of them, and each run returns the exact error trace to repair. successful program trains to completion, which is where execution time goes, so lower γs skips more of these long runs. Programs predicted to time out are never run, since timeout is the most costly outcome.

sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: The experiments answer three questions: (Q1) How accurately does MLE-World predict execution outcomes, and at what inference cost? (Section 6.1) (Q2) Does world model guided search improve submitted solutions, and do predicted outputs and the exploration bonus each help? (Section 6.2) (Q3) Does confidence identify unreliable predictions, and what tradeoff between quality and execution cost does gating achieve? (Section 6.3) Our main experiments use the same 17 of the 22 MLE-bench Lite tasks (Chan et al., 2025): following Yang et al. (2026a), we exclude five tasks on which our agents rarely make progress (task selection and statistics of the training data in Appendix A). sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: Limitations. Our main evaluation is in distribution: new programs on 17 tasks seen in finetuning (Appendix E). On three tasks excluded from finetuning, the 4B MLE-World, without reasoning, still predicts terminal output more accurately than much larger prompted models (53.3% versus 42.1% for DeepSeek with reasoning and 21.1% for Coder; Appendix R). This opens generalizable world model as future work, for example by adding reasoning or scaling up the model. Training uses about 500,000 prior executions, including earlier trajectories from 9B agent but no reported runs, favoring settings with accumulated logs. Zero shot baselines and Base AIDE lack this task knowledge; nonparametric corpus baselines trail MLE-World  (Table 1)  , while Base AIDE with corpus access remains untested. Real execution determines final scores; prediction errors can misdirect search. Timeouts are the least accurately predicted outcome, and missed timeout still costs full run; improving runtime prediction is future work. Conclusion. 4B model finetuned on logged executions predicts the outcomes of new programs more accurately than much larger prompted models, at 131,061 less GPU inference time. This makes test time scaling affordable for MLE agents: all five world model guided policies have higher observed mean percentiles than the agent without world model. Gating reduces real execution time by 3040% while broadly maintaining performance.

sections.content: LLMs are part of the method: Qwen3.5 models generate agent programs and Qwen3-Coder-Next judges outputs. sections.title: D TARGET ABLATION
sections.content: MLE-World predicts an exception class and validation metric alongside the terminal log (Section 4). This ablation asks whether these fields add information or merely duplicate what the log already contains. Setup. We fix the backbone, training corpus, split, and decoding, and vary only the target. Starting from terminal output plus submission flag, we add the exception class and then the validation metric. We also compare untrimmed logs with the default window of the first and last 2,500 characters, and we train target of metric plus submission flag with no terminal output. To keep each run affordable, the variants train on subset of 49,791 programs drawn from nine of the tasks and are scored against executed ground truth on 450 held out programs from those nine tasks  (Table 8)  . Absolute scores are therefore not comparable with Table 1. Little observed difference from trimming. We observed little difference between the 2,500 character window and untrimmed logs (terminal output 59.4% vs. 59.5%, exception class 71.7% vs. 71.4%; Table 8). With one training run per condition, these point estimates do not establish equivalence. Structured fields improve the log itself. Adding the exception class and then the validation metric raises agreement on terminal output from 59.4% to 62.8%, exception class agreement from 71.7% to 75.3%, and crash class agreement from 64.8% to 69.1%. Predicting explicit outcome fields also makes the generated log more accurate, rather than serving only as separate output. Dropping the log loses coverage and feedback. target of the metric alone reaches the highest metric precision (90.0%) but predicts metric for only 77.0% of cases with numeric reference, compared with 89.5% for the full target. It also provides no error trace for debugging. The full target gives up 1.0 point of precision for 12.5 points of recall and the feedback from logs the agent needs to repair failures. sections.title: E DEDUPLICATION AND HOLDOUT CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Deduplication. Agents rarely resubmit byte identical code; repeated attempts usually differ only in comments or formatting. We therefore key each program on hash of its Python token stream with comments and blank lines removed and indentation and line breaks normalized. Programs that differ only in comments, spacing, or blank lines share key; any change to identifiers, literals, or structure does not. Programs that fail to tokenize fall back to hash of their raw bytes. Before deduplication, we drop executions whose outcome reflects the harness rather than the program, such as GPU contention, host memory limits, or network failures. Deduplication then collapses 757,186 executions to 602,741. When the same program produced different outcomes across runs (for example, timeout in one run and clean finish in another), we keep one representative per outcome rather than an arbitrary winner. 16 MLE-World Table 8: Target ablation. All scores are percentages. Terminal output measures semantic agreement; exception/crash measure exact class agreement inferred from logs, with no exception included and crash restricted to jointly crashing cases. Metric precision uses 10% relative tolerance on commonly answered cases; recall is the fraction of cases with numeric reference receiving metric. Dashes indicate undefined scores from logs. From the 602,741 deduplicated executions we remove 43,836 on tasks outside our 17, 33,591 whose output contains progress bar (agents are told not to print them), 13,121 whose validation metric cannot be resolved unambiguously, 11,549 cut short by the agents overall deadline and logged as timeouts, and 1,888 with harness failures, invalid stage labels, or mislabeled interrupts. This leaves 498,756 executions. Holdout. From these 498,756 executions, we sample 100 programs per task, balanced across agent stages (draft, improve, debug) and between fast (5 s) and slow executions. We draw only programs without detected exact or near duplicate among the other programs of their task (procedure below), then remove the sampled programs from training. The remaining 497,056 executions form the training set. Near duplicates. Exact keys miss programs that differ only in identifier names or in few edits. We therefore replace identifiers with placeholders and treat two programs as duplicates when their identifier normalized abstract syntax trees hash identically, and as near duplicates when MinHash with locality sensitive hashing estimates Jaccard similarity of at least 0.9 between their identifier normalized token shingles (128 permutations in 16 bands of 8 rows, within each task). No exact or near duplicates were detected between holdout and training under this procedure. The probabilistic MinHash/LSH search can miss similar pairs; it does not rule out semantic similarity or overlap across tasks. Shared tasks. Held out programs are new, but their tasks also appear in training. This mirrors model based RL, where world model is trained and evaluated in the same environment and must predict the outcome of new actions, not new environments (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Janner et al., 2019). Here the task is the environment and executing program is an action: an agent writes hundreds of new programs for the task it is solving, so MLE-World must predict unseen programs within known tasks.

sections.title: JUDGE PROMPT AND VALIDATION
sections.content: What the judge decides. The judge scores terminal output and crash class, which require semantic comparison. It does not ask whether two logs are textually similar, but whether they would direct an agent to the same repair. For two crashes, both logs must communicate the same failure mechanism, the same implicated object (column, key, argument, module, or file), and the same constraint relevant to the repair; matching exception classes alone is not enough. For two successful runs, it compares the headline validation result, allowing 15% relative gap. Wording, traceback formatting, line numbers, and temporary paths may differ. The full prompt is reproduced below. Development. The prompt was developed iteratively by an LLM coding agent (GPT-5.6 Sol), which proposed revisions, ran the judge, and inspected its errors. Development used only separate development set: 120 natural cases and 64 controlled cases, each presented in both orders (128 pairs). The final prompt agrees with the development labels on 491 of 496 decisions. Held out test. Before prompt development began, we froze test set of 120 cases, stratified by failure type: 40 crashes with the same exception class, 15 with different classes, 15 missed crashes, 10 false crashes, 20 clean runs, and 20 truncated outputs, drawn from predictions of MLE-World, Coder, and DeepSeek. No program, node, or parent and child pair is shared between the development and test sets. The prompt was selected before any test input was viewed. Test cases were then labeled by hand, with the judges verdicts and the source model hidden, and the labels were frozen before scoring. Table 13 reports agreement over three judge requests per case. sections.content: The gate uses one pair of raw pmax thresholds at every stage: γs when MLE-World predicts success and γf when it predicts failure other than timeout. The two thresholds differ for two reasons. First, predicted successes and predicted failures have different pmax distributions, so they trade prediction error for skipped runtime differently (Figure 9), and single threshold would place them at different operating points: about 15% error requires γs = 0.90 for successes but only γf = 0.83 for failures. Second, they differ in cost. Predicted successes, two thirds of them Improve programs, are the long runs (median 115 s), so we want to skip as many of them as possible. Predicted failures, mostly Debug programs, usually crash within seconds (median 3 s), so running them is cheap and returns the exact error trace to repair. Predicted timeouts are never run (the timeout skip, Section 5.2): real run of program that times out occupies the executor for the full time limit and blocks the search, only to confirm failure the prediction already reports. Holdout tradeoff. We propose thresholds using 1,700 programexecution records held out from world-model finetuning (Section 6.1). These records are separate from agent evaluation trajectories. skipped success counts as an error when its predicted validation score is more than 5% away from the real one; skipped failure counts as an error when it names the wrong exception or the wrong cause to fix. sections.content: MLE-bench compares each final submission with the competitions human leaderboard. Its medals use Kaggles thresholds: gold requires the top 10% of teams on leaderboards with fewer than 100 teams, the top 10 on leaderboards with 100249 teams, and the top 10 plus 0.2% of all teams (rounded down) otherwise. Ten of our 17 leaderboards have more than 1,000 teams, where gold means roughly the top 1%. Leaderboard percentile instead measures the share of entries submission beats. We use percentile as the primary metric because medal rates are all or nothing: 12 of our 17 tasks never yield gold, while one task with small leaderboard yields more than half of all golds. Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) likewise rank agents by percentile because medal thresholds amplify noise and hide progress on hard tasks, and Foster et al. (2026) report continuous normalized score. Tables 21 and 22 break down the 306 final submissions of the six earlier 8 ungated policies by task and by policy. One task supplies more than half of all golds. Detecting-insults has leaderboard of 50 teams, so gold means the top five. Seventeen of its 18 submissions win gold; only one Fusion seed misses. The task accounts for 17 of the 31 golds and adds up to three golds, or 5.9 points of gold rate, to every policy without separating them. Most tasks never produce medal. Twelve tasks yield no gold in any submission and nine yield no medal of any kind, so medal rates ignore them. Percentile still separates policies on these tasks. Means for each policy range from 0.0 to 36.6 on mlsp-2013-birds, where three policies never produce valid submission, and from 2.9 to 53.9 on English text normalization, where single submission earns medal. Where golds occur, single seed decides them. On the other four gold tasks, gold requires the 98.7th to 99.1st percentile or the best leaderboard score. On aerial-cactus, 150 teams share perfect AUC of 1.0, so gold requires exactly 1.0: submission scoring 0.99996 ranks at the 87.7th percentile and wins no medal. With three seeds per task, one seed moves policys gold rate by 2.0 points. Gold rate can reverse the ranking. Base AIDE has twice Fusions gold rate (11.8% versus 5.9%; paired difference 5.9 points), yet Fusion submits valid solutions more often (96.1% versus 78.4%) and reaches higher mean percentile (+10.4 points). Pairwise exceeds Fusion in gold rate (+9.8 points) but trails it in mean percentile (4.4 points). Table 22 shows why. Fusions three golds contribute 5.9 of its 47.2 percentile points, and its 46 other valid submissions, at mean 45.8th percentile, contribute 41.3. Pairwises eight golds contribute 15.4 of its 42.8 points, but its 39 other valid submissions average only the 35.8th percentile, and its four invalid submissions score zero. Percentile has its own limit. Where leaderboard scores cluster, small score gains move percentile sharply: on English text normalization, accuracy 0.964 ranks at the 6th percentile and 0.990 at the 47th. Averaging over 17 equally weighted tasks limits the influence of any one leaderboard. We therefore base conclusions on mean percentile and report medal rates only for comparison with MLE-bench. 38 MLE-World Table 21: Medals by task. New tasks can reuse familiar execution operations: loading images, transforming tensors, and adapting pretrained models. Failures in these shared operations may remain predictable even when the data and prediction target change  (Table 24)  . Task-specific geometry, labels, and metrics introduce less familiar behavior. Shared code therefore offers plausible route to transfer, though training family ablations are needed to establish its role. Results and limitations.
